seriesStmt.p: Machine readable texts of the unpublished correspondence of James Joyce

msIdentifier.repository: Beinecke Rare Book & Manuscript Library, Yale University

projectDesc.p: James Joyce's unpublished correspondence, collected, annotated, and made available as a digital edition

div.p: Dear Pound: I saw the doctor today. He has now prescribed glasses for protracted work: right eye, +6, left eye +7. As regards cylindrical lenses he says I can try them if I wish and I shall do so as soon as funds permit their purchase. He says that in this country the American theory of astigmatism has not found favour but that that question is not the chief one with me. He supposes that an osteopath is an orthopedist and gave me the name of one here. Before calling on him however I shall wait for your confirmation of this. He persists in his opinion that iridectomy is necessary. He even said that now the eye is not so easy to operate as it was before. I understand that there is a tendency to iris bombans . The main question seems to my lay mind to be this: can synechia be lessened by other means than iridectomy. He says it is out of the question. I think however that the rheumatic infection, which as you say is not local seeing that I had it first in deltoid and biceps and last year in the back, might be lessened if not eliminated by some radical cure. Do you know whether the bacillus has been isolated? I think it was by an English scientist named Paignton. I cling desperately to the opinion that the iris would loosen its grip on the lens behind if the rheumatic infection could be got rid of. The worst of iridectomy seems to be that it needs to be done more than once. Ahi! He says the iritis has now subsided but his point of view is that in the next attack the cohesion consequent on exudation will be so strong as to negative the mydriatic effect of atropine altogether and endanger the sight. Devil take my absurd eyes! I am for the moment better and waiting for news from your New York specialist . Today for instance I had a dull feeling in the eye – not actually pain – and now the rain has come. In that case it would seem that the cohesion (I think it is called attachment) is elastic and what can become worse can become better – in theory. I have now discontinued the atropine. It dilated the pupil but not much. I ought to tell you also that the last flat I lived in here was very damp.

I spoke to some people here about your new review and hope I may be able to get a few subscribers, when you tell me the name and where it is to be bought. I hope you were not dissatisfied with my letter. In the meantime you can put my name into your list of future contributors.
I am getting on with Ulysses but am disinclined today a little on account of this depressing diagnosis. Needless to say it is a Friday and the thirteenth of the month also.

note.p: In his long letter to JJ of 17 March 1917, Pound, full of medical recommendations based partly on his own former eye problems, urged JJ to explore the benefits of treating “inharmonic astigmatism” with “cylindrical lenses, such as you should find in any opticians test room, twisting them about in the double grooved frames to see if they give any relief”. He also wondered if there was “a trained osteopath in Zurich” (“not a quack but one who has taken his proper degree”) who might provide relief by having JJ’s “vertebra set right side up and thus relieving blood or nerve pressures.” In particular, Pound hoped to put JJ in touch with George Milbry Gould (see below), an American ophthalmologist who had treated Pound in Philadelphia years earlier (Pound/Joyce 100-02).

John Quinn in New York was also drawn into consultations over JJ’s eyes. He wrote Nora Barnacle on 25 May 1917 that, given his own “experience in picking out specialists in medicine as well as in law,” he felt JJ should “get the best eye specialist or two of them that he can possibly get in Switzerland,” and not “take the advice of any casual friend … or personal friend of his.” After this side-thrust at Pound, man of many advices, Quinn added that, while he didn’t wish to disagree with Pound about Dr. Gould (in fact he considered Gould a crank), he had “a profound mistrust of a man three thousand miles away advising on a condition that may be as acute or as critical or painful as glancoma [sic] may be” (Pound/Joyce 99). For an account of Pound’s and Quinn’s attempted medical interventions, see Pound/Joyce 96-102.

div.note: Synechia, or an attachment between the iris and the lens capsule, could result from exudation caused by iritis. Medical treatment sought to prevent synechiae by keeping the pupil dilated through the mydriatic (or dilating) effects of atropine. Iridectomy was “urgently called for where the condition of iris bombans [swelling] exists” (George Andreas Berry, “Eye,” Encyclopedia Britannica, 11th ed., vol. X [Cambridge University Press, 1910], 97).
For JJ’s eye problems and his belief that they might be connected with an earlier attack of rheumatic fever, see JJ to Pound, 19 July 1915, notes.

JJ merges here the names of two English medical researchers, the physician Frederick J. Poynton (1869-1943) and the pathologist Alexander Paine (1866-1933), who coauthored, among other papers on the bacteriology of rheumatism, “The Etiology of Rheumatic Fever,” Lancet 156 (22 and 29 September 1900): 861-69, 932-35.

JJ suffered a severe attack of glaucoma in August 1917, prompting his ophthalmologist, Professor Ernst Sidler, to perform an iridectomy on his right eye at the Zurich Augenklinik a few days later. Resulting exudation from the eye during convalescence permanently reduced JJ’s vision (Ellmann, JJ 417). Atropine is a substance found in the potentially toxic nightshade belladonna, of which JJ was aware. The term “belladonna” occurs at least twice in both Ulysses and in Finnegans Wake (U 16.347, 18.576; FW 450.32, 585.24).

George Milbry Gould (1848-1922) was a noted ophthalmologist and prolific author who practiced in Philadelphia before settling in Ithaca, NY, and Atlantic City, NJ, in later years. He was noted for his theories of eye strain and his innovations with bifocal lenses. He was the author of many medical dictionaries and Concerning Lafcadio Hearn (Philadelphia: George W. Jacobs and Company, 1908), in which he concluded that Hearn’s “choice of subjects and methods of literary workmanship, and every line he wrote, were dictated and ruled by his … enormous monocular myopia” (147). Gould had once helped Pound’s vision by correcting his glasses prescription (Pound/Joyce 100-102). This may have been in the summer of 1910 when Pound, visiting his family in Pennsylvania, wrote to a friend: “I’m writing in the semi obscurity resultant upon drops which an oculust [sic] has squirted into my visual organs” (Ezra Pound and Margaret Cravens: A Tragic Friendship, 1910-1912, ed. Omar Pound and Robert Spoo [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1988], 46.) In June 1917, Gould finally responded to Pound’s requests for advice by stating, with thunderous obviousness, that JJ “should have gone to some trustworthy ophthalmic surgeon and been treated perhaps operated upon” (Pound/Joyce 120).

Pound began work for The Little Review in 1917 as its foreign editor. John Quinn made an annual subsidy to the magazine of £150, which Pound spread among the authors who contributed to the magazine, taking only a modest sum for himself, as it would have “spoiled the spirit of the thing if I had taken more than £60 out of the first year’s subsidy” (The Selected Letters of Ezra Pound to John Quinn, 1915-1924, ed. Timothy Materer [Durham, NC: Duke University Press, 1991], 165). Founded in Chicago in 1914 and edited by Margaret Anderson and Jane Heap, The Little Review moved to New York in 1917 and became one of the chief outlets for experimental writing and international art, publishing the work of Djuna Barnes, T.S. Eliot, Wyndham Lewis, Mina Loy, Francis Picabia, Dorothy Richardson, May Sinclair, Gertrude Stein, W.C. Williams, W.B. Yeats, Hans Arp, Marcel Duchamp, Fernand Léger, and many others. The Little Review serialized JJ’s Ulysses between 1918 and 1920, discontinuing installments when the editors were convicted of obscenity in a New York court for publishing the portion of the “Nausicaa” episode depicting Leopold Bloom masturbating at the seashore.

While preparing the May 1917 number of The Little Review (his début as foreign editor), Pound wrote JJ on 29 March 1917 to request “SOMETHING from you, even if it is only 500 words.” If JJ had no creative work on hand, Pound wanted at least “a note, of general good wishes, saying you are ill, but hope to send something soon” (Pound/Joyce 103-04). JJ replied on 9 April 1917 that he had nothing quite ready – an excerpt from the “Scylla and Charybdis” episode of Ulysses would “suffer by excision” – and, unfortunately, he had “very little imagination” (LI 101). He enclosed a note of sixty-seven words that was duly printed in The Little Review, vol. 4, no. 2 (June 1917): 26, expressing approval of the magazine’s “new plans” and hoping “to send you something very soon – as soon, in fact, as my health allows me to resume work.”
